title: The lane
hookLine: monks walk a straight path of twenty or thirty paces, back and forth

lines: A SWEPT PATH BETWEEN THE TREES.
cards: To the car. To the kitchen. To the meeting you're late for.
Ordinary walking is about the destination; the walk itself is dead time, filled with a phone or a podcast. Now a forest monastery in Thailand at dusk.
Between the trees runs a narrow, swept path of sand, maybe twenty or thirty steps long. A monk walks slowly to the end, stops, turns, and walks back. And again.
For an hour. He's not going anywhere. That's the point.

teach.b: Today's word is cankama: the walking path, and the practice of walking up and down on it. It's old.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA WALKING UP AND DOWN.
teach.b: In the Pali texts the Buddha is often found walking up and down in the open air, sometimes late into the night, and monks go to find him on his walking path.
The monastic rules describe walking paths and even covered walking halls, so monks could practice in the rain.
At Bodh Gaya, tradition marks a spot where the Buddha is said to have walked back and forth in the weeks after his awakening. Why a straight lane, and why so short?
Because a lane removes the destination. On a real walk the mind is always leaning ahead: the corner, the car, the next thing.
On twenty or thirty paces there's nothing ahead but the end of the lane, and then you turn around.
With no errand, the mind can finally settle into the walking itself: the feel of the foot, the shift of weight, the ground.
Walking meditation is sometimes treated as the lesser cousin of sitting, but teachers give it reasons of its own. It's easier when you're sleepy. It helps when the body is restless.

And it's a bridge: you can't sit cross-legged in a grocery store, but you can walk with attention anywhere. In forest monasteries a monk may walk his lane for hours. For the next six days, you'll learn to walk like this.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks and nuns practice walking meditation on a straight path, often twenty to thirty paces long, walking slowly back and forth, sometimes alternating with sitting.

o: a short path walked back and forth with care
a slow stroll through a monastery garden
a long pilgrimage on foot to a holy site

games.q: what's inside the practice — tap the pairs.
p: where tradition marks the Buddha's walk

s: walking meditation is a modern invention
the Pali texts often find the Buddha walking up and down in the open air.
the lane is short so the mind has nowhere to lean toward
with no errand ahead, the mind settles into the walking itself.
walking meditation can help when you're sleepy
it's easier than sitting when the mind is dull or the body restless.

games.q: you're walking your lane and the mind starts planning tomorrow. what do you do?
o: stop and write the plan down.
games.why: on the lane there's nowhere to get to: come back to the feel of the next step.

practice: If you can, stand at one end of a few paces of floor, a hallway or a quiet corner, feel your feet on the ground, and let your hands rest in front or behind you.

Walk slowly to the other end, stop for a breath, turn, and walk back, eyes lowered a few steps ahead; when the mind runs off, feel the next step. If you can't stand, feel your feet on the floor from your chair.

wordCard.voice: Cankama. The walking path, and the practice of walking back and forth on it with attention.

orig.note: Pali: the walking path, and walking up and down on it.

carryVoice: Your line: nowhere to get to. The lane is short on purpose. That's day one hundred seventeen.
